screens.title: The residual stream

$\operatorname{LN}(\Delta_2)$, the MLP 1 output alone

screens.title: How big each write is
screens.prose: The bars give the length (norm) of the embedding, of each update and of the final stream at position 6. The five terms have lengths that add to 25.27, yet the final stream is only 12.20 long.
screens.question: Why is the final stream shorter than the sum of the lengths?

options.text: The updates point in different directions, so they partly cancel
Layer norm shrinks the stream after each addition
options.why: In a pre-norm block the norm acts on the copy a part reads, never on the stream.

options.text: Some of the updates are lost along the way

hints.text: When is the length of a sum the sum of the lengths?
Only when every vector points the same way.

explain.text: By the triangle inequality, $\lVert \mathbf x_4 \rVert \le$ the sum of the lengths, with equality only when all terms line up. Here 12.20 against 25.27: the writes are big, and they partly cancel.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from seq_ops_l4 import attn_update, mlp_update


def stream_trace(tokens, model, h):
    tokens = np.asarray(tokens)
    x = model['E'][tokens] + model['P'][:len(tokens)]
    trace = [x]
    for p in model['blocks']:
        x = x + attn_update(x, p, h).data
        trace.append(x)
        x = x + mlp_update(x, p).data
        trace.append(x)
    return trace


def update_norms(trace):
    return np.array([np.linalg.norm(trace[k] - trace[k - 1], axis=-1) for k in range(1, len(trace))])

mutants.source:
import numpy as np
from nt_ops_l2 import layernorm
from seq_ops_l4 import attn_update, mlp_update


def ablate_sublayer(tokens, model, k, h=4):
    tokens = np.asarray(tokens)
    x = model['E'][tokens] + model['P'][:len(tokens)]
    j, removed = 0, 0
    for p in model['blocks']:
        for part in (lambda x: attn_update(x, p, h), lambda x: mlp_update(x, p)):
            j += 1
            w = part(x).data
            x = x + w
            if j == k:
                removed = w
    x = x - removed
    return layernorm(x, model['lnf_g'], model['lnf_b']).data @ model['U'] + model['c']

screens.prose: Edge case: set $\mathbf W_O$, $\mathbf b_O$, $\mathbf W_2$ and $\mathbf b_2$ of block 2 to zero. Both its writes are then zero vectors.
screens.question: What does block 2 now output?

options.text: Its input, unchanged: the identity
A vector of zeros of the same shape
options.why: You thought of the block as replacing its input. Its writes are zero, so it adds nothing.

options.text: The layer-normalised copy of its input
options.why: The norms shape only what the parts read. The stream itself is never normalised inside a block.

hints.text: What is $\mathbf x + \mathbf 0$?
Both writes are zero.
The block passes its input through.

feedback.generic: Not quite. A block outputs its input plus its writes.

explain.text: A residual block whose parts write zero is the identity. That is why a deep stack can start near the identity and learn each correction, as the residual block in `cnn` l11 did.

screens.title: Every layer reads and writes
screens.prose: With $L$ parts the stream is $$\mathbf x_L = \mathbf x_0 + \sum_{\ell=1}^{L} \Delta_\ell, \qquad \Delta_\ell = F_\ell(\mathbf x_{\ell-1}).$$ So $\partial \mathbf x_L / \partial \mathbf x_\ell = \mathbf I + {}$ terms through the later parts.
screens.question: Why does a gradient from the loss reach part 1 even when the later parts' own gradients are tiny?

options.text: Each addition passes it on through the identity term
Layer norm rescales the gradient back up
options.why: The identity path holds without any norm; layer norm only shapes what each part reads.

options.text: The causal mask keeps it from leaking away
options.why: The mask decides which positions mix. It plays no part in passing gradients back through depth.

feedback.correct: Right: the $\mathbf I$ in every Jacobian is a direct line to every layer.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look at the $\mathbf I$ in the derivative.

explain.text: Every part sits on its own branch beside the identity path, as `cnn` l11's identity path did for one block. So the loss reaches each part directly, and each part reads every earlier write.

The output of the last block only

options.text: The training loss curve
options.why: The curve says how training went on average, not what went wrong on this headline.

Each part's write is one term of the sum.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The final vector is a sum; start by sizing its terms.

explain.text: Because the stream is a sum, each part's contribution can be measured on its own. Reading a model this way is where interpretability begins: `interp` L1 does it with the logit lens.

ideas: The residual stream is a running sum, $\mathbf x_L = \mathbf x_0 + \sum_\ell \Delta_\ell$: each part reads it through its layer norm and writes back by addition.
Nothing is overwritten: the embedding is still a term of the final stream. Writes that point different ways partly cancel.
Each addition passes the gradient straight to every part. Removing one write and rerunning (ablation) shows what that part does.
